definition: In this historical ethical usage, sensus communis refers to a shared common sense by which basic moral principles are immediately recognized. In early English moral philosophy, it named the supposed source of first moral truths and was linked with intuitional or common-sense morality.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record EthicalT; pinned source text

reasons: The packet supports Herbert of Cherbury’s use of sensus communis for moral first principles in early English philosophy, but it does not support the added claim that this was a ‘shared’ common sense.
The wording ‘source of first moral truths’ goes beyond the packet’s phrasing, which speaks of moral first principles and immediate apprehension, not a source of truth in that explicit form.

The packet only states that in the beginning of English philosophy moral first principles were regarded as principles of the *sensus communis* by Herbert of Cherbury; it does not explicitly define sensus communis as a “shared common sense by which basic moral principles are immediately recognized.”
The packet does not explicitly support the claim that sensus communis was “the supposed source of first moral truths.”

The packet supports a connection to “intuitional or common-sense morality” (Herbert of Cherbury is said to found this school), but the provided definition adds additional specifics (shared immediate recognition; source of first moral truths) that are not explicitly present in the packet.
